If this sit- uation arises, the member should therefore disclose the fact that he has an interest in the matter in a meeting called under the Open Meetings Act, and recuse him- self not only from voting, but from any participation in the matter. There is an exception to the prohi- bition for fees for services, but the exception is applicable only if the fee is for services rendered in a capacity other than as a public servant. A member of the Board of Vocational Nurse Examiners should not offer continuing education courses for profit for vocational nurses seeking license renewal. EAO 257. In a situation in which a member of the governing board of a state agency has a personal or private interest in a matter pending before the board, section 572.058 of the Government Code requires that the board member dis- close the interest and recuse himself from participation in the matter. Section 572.058 does not require the board member to divest himself of the interest. EAO 256. See also EAO 218. The Texas Certified Self-Insurer Guaranty Association (TCSGA) board of directors is not part of the executive branch of state government. Although the TCSGA is statutorily cre- ated, its members are private employers who desire to become certified self-insurers for purposes of workersΓÇÖ compensation benefits for their employees. Labor Code ┬º 407.121. TCSGA receives no state appropriated funds. In light of these features of the TCSGA, we do not think the legislature intended that TCSGA be considered part of the executive branch of state government. Therefore, because TCSGA is not a state agency for purposes of chapter 572, the requirements of section 572.058(a) do not apply to state officers who are members of the TCSGA board when they are acting in their capacity as TCSGA board members. Because we have determined that the TCSGA is not a state agency for purposes of chapter 572, the revolving door prohibition is inapplica- ble to the self-insurer members of the TCSGA board. EAO 179. See also EAO 142. Sec. 572.059. INDEPENDENCE OF STATE AND LOCAL OFFICERS ACTING IN LEGISLATIVE CAPACITY (a) 	In this section, ΓÇ£legislative measureΓÇ¥ includes: T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 95 Ch. 572 Government Code (1) 	a bill, resolution, order, or other proposal to adopt, enact, amend, or repeal a statute, ordinance, rule, or policy of general application; (2) 	a proposal to adopt, enact, amend, or repeal, or to grant a variance or other exception to, a zoning ordinance; or (3) 	a proposed constitutional amendment or charter amendment subject to a vote of the electorate. (b) 	For purposes of Subsection (a), a measure that is applicable to a class or subset of persons or matters that is defined in general terms without naming the particular persons or matters is a measure of general application. (c) 	To protect the independence of state and local officers acting in a legislative capacity, a state or local officer, whether elected or appointed, including a member of the governing body of a school district or other political subdivision of this state, may not be subject to disciplinary action or a sanction, penalty, disability, or liability for: (1) 	an action permitted by law that the officer takes in the officerΓÇÖs official capacity regarding a legis- lative measure; (2) 	proposing, endorsing, or expressing support for or opposition to a legislative measure or taking any action permitted by law to support or oppose a legislative measure; (3) 	the effect of a legislative measure or of a change in law proposed by a legislative measure on any person; or (4) 	a breach of duty, in connection with the memberΓÇÖs practice of or employment in a licensed or regulated profession or occupation, to disclose to any person information, or to obtain a waiver or consent from any person, regarding: (A) the officerΓÇÖs actions relating to a legislative measure; or (B) the substance, effects, or potential effects of a legislative measure. Added by Acts 2003, 78 th Leg., ch. 1206, Sec. 1, eff. June 20, 2003. Sec. 572.060. SOLICITATION OF OR RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING CONTRIBUTIONS TO CHARITABLE ORGANIZATIONS AND GOVERNMENTAL ENTITIES (a) 	Unless otherwise prohibited by the Code of Judicial Conduct, a state officer or state employee may: (1) 	solicit from any person a contribution to: (A) an organization that: (i) 	is exempt from income taxation under Section 501(a), Internal Revenue Code of 1986, by being listed under Section 501(c)(3) of that code; (ii) 	does not attempt to influence legislation as a substantial part of the organizationΓÇÖs activ- ities; and (iii) 	has not elected under Section 501(h), Internal Revenue Code of 1986, to have that sub- section apply to the organization; or (B) a governmental entity; or T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 96 Ch. 572 Government Code (2) 	recommend to any person that the person make a contribution to an organization or entity described by Subdivision (1). (b) 	A monetary contribution solicited or recommended as provided by Subsection (a) must: (1) 	be paid or made directly to the charitable organization or governmental entity by the person making the contribution; (2) 	be in the form of a check, money order, or similar instrument payable to the charitable organiza- tion or governmental entity; or (3) 	be in the form of a deduction from a state employeeΓÇÖs salary or wage payment under the state employee charitable campaign under Subchapter I, Chapter 659. (c) 	A contribution solicited or recommended as provided by Subsection (a) that is not a monetary contri- bution must be delivered directly to the charitable organization or governmental entity by the person making the contribution. (d) 	A contribution paid as provided by Subsection (b) or delivered as provided by Subsection (c) is not: (1) 	a political contribution to, or political expenditure on behalf of, the state officer or state employee for purposes of Title 15, Election Code; (2) 	an expenditure for purposes of Chapter 305; or (3) 	a benefit to the state officer or state employee for purposes of Sections 36.08 and 36.09, Penal Code. Ethics CommΓÇÖn Op. No. 571 (2022), quoting the State of Texas Procurement and Contract Management Guide. Unlike the other Chapter 572 ΓÇ£revolving doorΓÇ¥ prohibitions [in 572.054], this provision applies to all former state employees and does not merely prohibit for- mer state agency employees from working on particular matters in their new employment. Compare id. ┬º 572.054, with id. ┬º 572.069. Instead, it prohibits former state agency employees from accepting any employment from certain persons for two years, even if the private employ- ment is unrelated to anything they worked on during their state service. Based on the test of 1. Whether the purchase of the vendorΓÇÖs products was a procurement, 2. Whether the requestor participated in the procurement, and 3. Whether the procurement involved the vendor in question, the former state employee would not be able to work for the particular employer for two years after the contract was signed. EAO 626. See also, EAO 586 (2023), EAO 571 (2022), EAO 568 (2021), EAO 545 (2017). STATE EMPLOYEE MAY NOT BE EMPLOYED IF HE PARTICIPATED IN CONTRACTS. Requestor is an employee of HHSC who plans on leaving to join a company with several state contracts. He expects to help manage payments to the state each month as well as helping with eligibility and quality control, but will not engage with the state contracts with HHSC. These are different particular matters than his work with the HHSC, so neither 572.054 would apply. This is the first opinion to address a state contract negotiation that was not also a procurement, but the same principle applies ΓÇô if the requestor gave approval, advice or recommendation on whether to enter into a contract at all, he participated and would be prohibited from employment with the company for 2 years. EAO 600. See also, Revolving Door #2: EAO 496 (2011), EAO 397 (1998), EAO 364 (1997). Revolving Door #3: EAO 568 (2021), EAO 545 (2017). T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 97 Ch. 572 Government Code FORMER STATE EMPLOYEE MAY PROVIDE CONSULTING SERVICES. A former state employee became part-owner of a consulting business and that consulting business seeks to contract with one or more businesses that were involved in procurements that he participated in. Since the law specifies ΓÇ£employmentΓÇ¥ and the individual would be providing only consulting services through his own business, it is not prohibited by ┬º572.069. EAO 599. See also, EAO 582 (2022), EAO 572, EAO 545 (2017), Tex. AttΓÇÖy Gen. Op. No. GA-0292 at 4 (2005), Tex. AttΓÇÖy Gen. Op. No. DM- 409, at 5 (1996). Under 572.054(a): he must wait two years before appearing before or seeking to influence both the Commissioner of Education (officer of SBOE) and the PSF Corporation (because the Corporation board con- tains SBOE members). He would also be restricted with respect to TEA employees if they were also employees of the SBOE under the common law employee/er test. Under 572.069: he may not accept employment for two years from any person involved in any transactions which were subject to a ratification vote by the SBOE board during his tenure there. EAO 598. The requestor has reduced his work hours at a university where he works to pursue outside consulting projects. Since he will maintain his employment, he is not a ΓÇ£formerΓÇ¥ employee and thus the revolving door provisions do not apply. But elements of 572.051, Government Code and the 39.06, Penal Code might apply re: standards of conduct, ethics policies, or use of nonpublic information to gain a benefit. EAO 595. RECEIVING COMPENSATION AS EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR OF NON-PROFIT. The laws under the Ethics CommissionΓÇÖs jurisdiction would not prohibit a legislator from solely receiving compensation from the organization, provided that the compensation reflects the actual value of the legislatorΓÇÖs services and not because of his status as a public servant; the services are provided in a capacity other than as a public servant and as long as the legislatorΓÇÖs official position is not a reason for his employment by the organization; the compensation is not received in exchange for an official act as a public servant; and the compensation is neither a prohibited political contribution nor a gift, loan, or other prohib- ited expenditure by a registered lobbyist. A legislator should understand that the solicitation of contributions to an organization for which the legislator serves as executive director and from which the legislator receives compensation for services could be viewed as improper under certain circumstances. EAO 573 is even more interesting in that the commission specifically uses the definition of ΓÇ£personΓÇ¥ in Ch. 572 to include only for-profit businesses. The federal rule states that in order to avoid an appearance of impropriety, a fundraiser which accepts auction prizes and entertainment from corporate entities must raise at least three times the cost (or fair market value) of the auction items donated and entertainment provided. This rule is designed to keep corporations from donating costly items to a PAC for auction, but only valuing them or charging the PAC a minimal amount of money to obtain it. Then once the PAC auctions off the item for a large amount, the corporation has essentially just worked around making a prohibited corporate contribution of a large sum of money to that PAC. If the event does not raise that amount, then a complicated formula is required to refund portions of that money until it reaches the required benchmark. P ractice Notes Note: After the Texasn for Free Enterprise case (see below), the TEC acknowledged that it will no longer enforce subsection (a) above. After the Citizens United decision in 2010, corporate involvement in campaigns increased dramatically at all levels. But that decision isnΓÇÖt necessarily what allowed corporations to do so. Direct campaign expenditures (usually called independent expenditures on the federal level) were legal in Texas for years prior to Citizens United. The case merely brought the practice to light and cemented its place as a legitimate tool for corporations and labor organizations to get around corporate contribution prohibitions. The natural progression from corporate independent expenditures was to pool corporate money from multiple sources and make expenditures from a single source. From this idea, Super PACs arose and regulation followed, and some national organizations made headlines by using 501(c)(4) non-profit organizations to engage in political activity. One upside to this practice is that 501(c)(4)ΓÇÖs are tax exempt as long as their political activity does not cross a majority (50% +) threshold. The biggest advantage is that 501(c)(4) organizations do not have to disclose their contributors to the Federal Election Commission or the Texas Ethics Commission (ΓÇ£TECΓÇ¥). In fact, the IRS removed the require- ment that 501(c)(4) nonprofits disclose ΓÇ£largeΓÇ¥ donors who contribute over $5,000. So now, 501(c)(4)ΓÇÖs donΓÇÖt have to disclose their donors to anyone. The downside is the possible public perception of non-profits cheating the system. From 2012 to 2014, the term ΓÇ£dark moneyΓÇ¥ emerged to describe this practice in a negative connotation, and elected officials took notice. A number of bills were filed to address the issue, and Governor Abbott issued emergency declarations to pass meaningful ethics reform in both the 2015 and 2017 legislative sessions. However, a full omnibus reform never materialized even when the TEC was up for sunset review in 2025. In the meantime, the TEC made attempts to address issues at the regulatory level. Many of these changes were the result of the Ethics CommissionΓÇÖs considerable time spent in the courtroom defending itself and the laws under its jurisdiction, some of which are detailed below. case law Virden v. City of Austin, No. 21-50597 (5th Circuit decision Oct. 25, 2021) This case originated out of an Austin city council race in which the plaintiff challenged the constitutionality of a one year moratorium on collecting contributions as a city council candidate for election. See, e.g., Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1, 24, 44ΓÇô45 (1976) (per curiam). A contributor has a constitutionally protected right of association, typically expressed by donating money to candidates or political action committees (ΓÇ£PACsΓÇ¥). See id. at 24ΓÇô25. Texas Ethics Commission, 732 F. 3d 535 (5th Cir. 2013) Texans for Free Enterprise (TFE) was a political committee which, by its own admission, did not have any intention on making contributions to candidates but rather only made direct campaign expenditures. Based on the Citizens United decision, TFE sued the TEC and filed an injunction to keep the TEC from enforcing a long-standing pro- hibition on PACs accepting corporate contributions to use in political expenditures. TFE argued that this prohibi- tion under the circumstances violated the First Amendment as applied to TFE. Ultimately the 5th Circuit agreed, and as a result, the Ethics Commission announced that it would no longer enforce ┬º253.094(a), Election Code and ┬º253.003(b), Election Code in certain circumstances. This case led to the creation of Direct Campaign Expenditure- Only Committees in Texas, which operate like federal Super PACs in that they can accept and pool corporate money from multiple sources and then turn around and spend that money only on direct campaign expenditures supporting or opposing candidates/measures. These committees are still prohibited from using any of the corporate money to contribute to candidates. The issue of dark money contributions and expenditures is still a moving target in regards to regulation, but Ethics Commission rules ┬º22.5 and ┬º22.6 and some ethics opinions referenced below show the recent attempts by the Ethics Commission to reign in hidden political activity. Ex parte Ellis, 309 SW 3d 71 (Tex. Crim. App. 2010) Under this statute, a corporation can contribute money to support or oppose a measure, but only if it gives that money to an entity devoted exclusively to measures, i.e. an entity that does not contribute to candidates. A corporation vio- lates the law if it makes a contribution to a political committee for the purpose of supporting or opposing a measure if that political committee also contributes to candidates. The exclusivity aspect of the provision seems designed to prevent diversion of funds from an acceptable purpose (supporting or opposing a measure) to an unacceptable purpose (supporting or opposing a candidate). A corporation can be confident that it is following the law if the con- tribution is given to a political committee devoted exclusively to measures because that political committee cannot make a contribution to a candidate. And a corporation can be equally confident that a political contribution given to an entity that is not devoted exclusively to measures is a violation of the law unless authorized by another provision of the Election Code. That a particular candidate may be associated with the measure has no effect on this authorization. As we also explained above, it is true that a corporation may not make a political contribution with respect to a measure to a political committee that also contributes to candidates. That is so, regardless of whether or not a particular candidate is associated with the measure in question. T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 176 Ch. 253 Election Code We decide that the prohibition against making corporate political contributions on a measure to a mixed-purpose political committee is ΓÇ£closely drawn to match a sufficiently important interest.ΓÇ¥ This prohibition serves to prevent the diversion of corporate ΓÇ£measureΓÇ¥ money to candidates, and thus ensures that the prohibition against corporate contributions to candidates will not be circumvented. The law is narrowly drawn because it addresses a narrow aspect of political association while allowing corporations several alternate avenues for political expression with respect to measures. First and most obviously, a corporation may contribute to a political committee devoted exclu- sively to measures. Second, a corporation may create its own political committee, which can then solicit contributions from the corporationΓÇÖs shareholders, employees, and their families, and any contributions received may then be con- tributed without being subject to corporate limitations. Finally, a corporation may make independent expenditures (e.g., buy its own issue ads), make press releases, and otherwise have its agents directly engage in communication with respect to a measure (or a candidate, for that matter). Michigan Chamber of Commerce to state that prohibitions on independent expenditures by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment. The ruling upheld restrictions on corporate contributions directly to candidates but freed contributions and unions to spend directly on electioneering communications that advocate for the election or defeat of candidates. Peca, 12 S.W.3d 31 at 43 (Tex., 2000) ΓÇ£Though complexly phrased and structured, the Election Code has an unambiguous intended effect: an individual must report direct expenditures that total over $100 or the unreported expenditures become illegal and the spender may face civil and criminal penalties; if the spender reports the expenditures, he or she faces no penalties. As Peca argues, these provisions operate to impose a reporting requirement on direct campaign expenditures, rather than a ban or ceiling on those expenditures. Because in a candidate election the ultimate burden of these requirements is substantially similar to that of the federal reporting requirements, they fall into the genus of requirements that Buckley upheld as ΓÇ£a reasonable and minimally restrictive method of furthering First Amendment values by opening the basic processes of [the] election system to public view.ΓÇ¥ Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1 at 82 (1976).ΓÇ¥ Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1 (1976) (Overruled by McCutcheon v. FEC) In Buckley, the Court upheld limitations on the amount of money a person may contribute to another personΓÇÖs campaign but struck down limitations on independent expenditures (ΓÇ£direct campaign expendituresΓÇ¥ in Texas). Although a limitation upon the amount of money a person or group may contribute to a candidate or political committee ΓÇ£entails only a marginal restriction upon the contributorΓÇÖs ability to engage in free communication,ΓÇ¥ a limitation upon independent expenditures ΓÇ£heavily burdens core First Amendment expression.ΓÇ¥ The Court found that contribution limitations were sufficiently justified by the danger of corruption or the appearance of corruption, while these dangers were not sufficient to justify limitations on independent expenditures. ethics commissioN oPiNioNs CORPORATE SHAREHOLDERS MAY CAUSE WHOLE LLC TO BE CONSIDERED CORPORATE. EAO 581. See also, EAO 181 (1994), EAO 163 (1993), EAO 132 (1993). NONPROFIT 	PRO 	BONO 	LEGAL 	SERVICES TO 	CANDIDATES 	TO 	CHALLENGE 	LAWS UNDER TEC JURISDICTION ARE POLITICAL CONTRIBUTIONS. Legal services provided without charge to candidates or PACs are in-kind contributions. They are not considered permissible discounts under TEC rule 20.66 (which are allowable as long as they are provided across the spectrum in the usual and normal practice of the industry, with no favoritism for those in politics) because it must apply broadly to the industry as a whole. Here, the TEC defined the industry as ΓÇ£legal servicesΓÇ¥, and not ΓÇ£nonprofits that offer pro bono legal servicesΓÇ¥. EAO 580. See also, EAO 574 (2022), EAO 533 (2015), EAO 498 (2011), EAO 433 (2001), EAO 329 (1996), EAO 222 (1994), EAO 219 (1994), EAO 105 (1992). CORPORATE 	ADVERTISEMENTS 	COORDI- NATED WITH CANDIDATES & PARTY ARE PROHIBITED. If a person who is a former candidate for and former holder of a judicial office uses political con- tributions to pay a portion of the legal expenses for a def- amation lawsuit, the amount of proceeds subject to the prohibition on personal use is proportional to the amount of legal expenses paid with political contributions. With respect to any proceeds from the lawsuit, the amount that is proportional to the amount of legal expenses that are paid with political contributions must be paid into the personΓÇÖs political fund. EAO 499. See also EAO 498, EAO 478, EAO 224, EAO 248. LEGAL 	EXPENSES FOR 	CANDIDATE-BASED DEFAMATION 	LAWSUIT. 	The 	use 	of 	political T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 209 Ch. 253 Election Code contributions by a former candidate for and former holder of a judicial office to pay legal expenses he incurred in connection with a defamation lawsuit he brought in his status as a candidate would not constitute a conversion of contributions to personal use under section 253.035 of the Election Code. EAO 498. See also EAO 433, EAO 222, EAO 310, EAO 219, EAO 105, EAO 276, EAO 478, EAO 224, EAO 204. COMPENSATING COUNTY EMPLOYEE FOR VACATION TIME UNUSED DUE TO WORK OBLIGATIONS. Title 15 of the Election Code does not prohibit an officeholder from using political contributions to compensate a county employee for vacation time that the employee was unable to take due to carrying out his or her county responsibilities on assignments connected with the activities of the officeholderΓÇÖs office. The office- holder may use personal funds to make the payment to compensate the employee for the lost vacation time and may seek reimbursement from political contributions provided that the expenditure from personal funds is reported as required by title 15 of the Election Code. The court employee may accept the compensation at issue under section 36.10(a)(2) of the Penal Code. EAO 480. See also EAO 254. DEFENDING 	LAWSUIT 	FOR 	JUDICIAL MISCONDUCT. A contribution to a judge to defray expenses incurred in defending himself against charges of judicial misconduct is an ΓÇ£officeholder contributionΓÇ¥ for purposes of title 15 of the Election Code. A judge may use surplus political contributions to defray expenses incurred in defending himself against charges of judicial misconduct. EAO 433. See also EAO 310. CAMPAIGN 	MATERIALS 	PAID 	FOR 	AND REPORTED IN PREVIOUS CAMPAIGN. A candi- date is not required to report his use in a current cam- paign of materials paid for and reported in connection with a previous campaign, including campaign balloons with ΓÇ£re-electΓÇ¥ language. EAO 390. See also EAO 116, EAO 387, EAO 184. PERSONAL 	MONEY 	USED 	& 	REIMBURSED WITH COMMERCIALLY REASONABLE INTE- REST. A candidate or officeholder may use political con- tributions to reimburse himself or herself with interest at a commercially reasonable rate for political expenditures made from the candidateΓÇÖs or officeholderΓÇÖs personal funds. For judicial candidates, there is a cap on the total amount a judicial candidate may reimburse himself or herself from political contributions. The caps on reim- bursement set out in Election Code section 253.162 are the total amounts judicial candidates and officeholders may pay themselves to compensate themselves for politi- cal expenditures made from personal funds. Any interest paid is included in determining whether a candidate or officeholder has reached the applicable cap. EAO 375. See also EAO 349, EAO 258. LOANS 	TO 	FAMILY 	MEMBERS 	& 	USE 	OF CONTRIBUTIONS. Section 253.162(b) of the Election Code prohibits certain judicial candidates and office- holders from using political contributions to repay loans to a person related to the candidate or officeholder within the second degree of consanguinity, but is not retroactive to the repayment of a loan made before June 16, 1995. EAO 350. REPAYING BANK LOAN & REIMBURSEMENT LIMIT. The result of a candidateΓÇÖs use of political con- tributions to reimburse personal funds is that the polit- ical contributions become available for the candidateΓÇÖs unrestricted personal use. A loan repayment, in contrast, makes funds available to a third party. Therefore, a candidateΓÇÖs use of political contributions to repay a bank loan does not count toward the limit on reimbursement set out in Election Code section 253.162. EAO 389. See also EAO 258, EAO 230. EVENTS IN CONNECTION WITH ACTIVTIES AS JUDICIAL CANDIDATE OR OFFICEHOLDER. As long as the payments for social events are in connec- tion with a judgeΓÇÖs activities as a candidate or office- holder, the judge may use political contributions to make those payments. EAO 284. PAYING FOR CONTINUING LEGAL EDUCA- TION COURSES. A senior judge is a retired judge who elects to be a judicial officer subject to assignment. Therefore, payment for continuing legal education courses is connected with a senior judgeΓÇÖs duties as a holder of public office, and may be made from the judgeΓÇÖs surplus political contributions. EAO 279. See also EAO 196, 245; ┬º75.001, Government Code; Attorney General Opinion H-526 (1975). EXPENSES 	INCURRED 	IN 	CONNECTION WITH A COURSE RELATED TO THE JUDGEΓÇÖS DUTIES. A judge may use political contributions to pay expenses incurred in connection with a course of study related to the judgeΓÇÖs duties or activities of office (in this case in the preparation of a thesis required for a Masters of Law in the Judicial Process). EAO 247. PAYING STATE BAR DUES WITH CONTRI- BUTIONS. For judges required to be licensed to practice T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 210 Ch. 253 Election Code law in Texas, the payment of state bar dues is a purpose connected with the duties or activities of a judicial can- didate or officeholder. Consequently, such judicial candi- dates and officeholders may use political contributions to pay state bar dues without violating Election Code sec- tion 253.035, the ΓÇ£personal useΓÇ¥ prohibition. EAO 245. OFFSETTING COSTS OF CIVIL ACTION FILED WITH STATE BAR ASSOCIATION AGAINST AN OFFICEHOLDER. Grievances filed before the State Bar for alleged violations of provisions governing con- duct as a candidate are civil actions and political contri- butions may be used to defray the costs of responding to the grievance. EAO 222. See also, EAO 206. Sec. 253.1621. Code ┬º┬º253.002, 253.097, 254.036(f), and Subchapter C, ┬º┬º253.061, 253.062, 253.063) CANDIDATE 	OBLIGATION 	TO 	REPORT DIRECT CAMPAIGN EXPENDITURE. A candi- date is required to report a direct campaign expenditure (as opposed to a contribution) made to support him or her only if the candidate receives notice under sections 253.062(a)(1), 254.128(a), or 254.161 of the Election Code. Ed note: The group that made the direct campaign expenditure in question here had not filed an appoint- ment of campaign treasurer as a political committee and apparently was not required to file. Although the campaign treasurer of a political committee is required to give notice to a candidate of a direct expenditure the committee makes on a candidateΓÇÖs behalf, this require- ment is not applicable in this situation because there is no campaign treasurer subject to the requirement. The fact that no notice is required in the situation described may have been an unintended result of a 1993 change in the law that allowed a political committee to accept up to $500 in contributions or make up to $500 in expen- ditures before filing a campaign treasurer appointment. Previously, a political committee could not accept any political contributions or make any political expenditures without appointing a campaign treasurer. EAO 331. INDIVIDUAL 	THAT 	SPENDS 	FUNDS 	TO ENTERTAIN OTHERS TO SOLICIT CONTRI- BUTIONS FOR A CANDIDATE. If the expenditure is not a contribution, the money spent on the entertain- ment event is a direct campaign expenditure. If the host is an individual not acting in concert with another, and the direct campaign expenditure is more than $100, the individual must report the expenditure as if the person were a specific-purpose political committee. If the host is acting in concert with one or more other persons, the group of persons is a political committee and the direct expenditure is subject to the various requirements appli- cable to expenditures by political committees. sections.content: 398 MISCELLANEOUS PROVISIONS RELATING TO GOVERNMENTAL ENTITY REPORTING Section 2252.908, Government Code Sec. 2252.908. DISCLOSURE OF INTERESTED PARTIES. (a) 	In this section: (1) 	ΓÇ£Business entityΓÇ¥ means any entity recognized by law through which business is conducted, including a sole proprietorship, partnership, or corporation. (2) 	ΓÇ£Governmental entityΓÇ¥ means a municipality, county, public school district, or special-purpose district or authority. (3) 	ΓÇ£Interested partyΓÇ¥ means a person who has a controlling interest in a business entity with whom a governmental entity or state agency contracts or who actively participates in facilitating the contract or negotiating the terms of the contract, including a broker, intermediary, adviser, or attorney for the business entity. (4) 	ΓÇ£State agencyΓÇ¥ means a board, commission, office, department, or other agency in the executive, judicial, or legislative branch of state government. The term includes an institution of higher education as defined by Section 61.003, Education Code. (b) 	This section applies only to a contract of a governmental entity or state agency that: (1) 	requires an action or vote by the governing body of the entity or agency before the contract may be signed; (2) 	has a value of at least $1 million; or (3) 	is for services that would require a person to register as a lobbyist under Chapter 305. (c) 	Notwithstanding Subsection (b), this section does not apply to: (1) 	a sponsored research contract of an institution of higher education; (2) 	an interagency contract of a state agency or an institution of higher education; (3) 	a contract related to health and human services if: (A) the value of the contract cannot be determined at the time the contract is executed; and (B) any qualified vendor is eligible for the contract; (4) 	a contract with a publicly traded business entity, including a wholly owned subsidiary of the business entity; (5) 	a contract with an electric utility, as that term is defined by Section 31.002, Utilities Code; or (6) 	a contract with a gas utility, as that term is defined by Section 121.001, Utilities Code. (d) 	A governmental entity or state agency may not enter into a contract described by Subsection (b) with a business entity unless the business entity, in accordance with this section and rules adopted under this section, submits a disclosure of interested parties to the governmental entity or state agency at the time the business entity submits the signed contract to the governmental entity or state agency. Governmental Entity Reporting T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 399 (e) 	The disclosure of interested parties must be submitted on a form prescribed by the Texas Ethics Commission that includes: (1) 	a list of each interested party for the contract of which the contracting business entity is aware; and (2) 	a written, unsworn declaration subscribed by the authorized agent of the contracting business entity as true under penalty of perjury that is in substantially the following form: ΓÇ£My name is 	, my date of birth is 	, and my address is , 	, 	, 	, (Street) 	(City) 	(State) 	(Zip Code) . I declare under penalty of (Country) perjury that the foregoing is true and correct. Executed in 	County, State of 	, on the day of 	, 	. (Month) 	(Year) DeclarantΓÇ¥. (f) 	Not later than the 30 th day after the date the governmental entity or state agency receives a disclosure of interested parties required under this section, the governmental entity or state agency shall submit a copy of the disclosure to the Texas Ethics Commission. (f-1) A contract described by Subsection (b) entered into by a governmental entity or state agency is void- able for failure to provide the disclosure of interested parties required by this section only if: (1) 	the governmental entity or state agency submits to the business entity written notice of the busi- ness entityΓÇÖs failure to provide the required disclosure; and (2) 	the business entity fails to submit to the governmental entity or state agency the required disclo- sure on or before the 10 th business day after the date the business entity receives the written notice under Subdivision (1). (g) 	The Texas Ethics Commission shall adopt rules necessary to implement this section, prescribe the disclosure of interested parties form, and post a copy of the form on the commissionΓÇÖs Internet website. Code, ┬º46.5 Governmental Entity Reporting T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 400 P ractice Note The 2023 bill which added subsection (f-1) also stated that if a court case is pending as of the effective date ( June 9, 2023) in which a party challenges the validity of a contract under subsection (b), the court may require the govern- mental entity/agency to provide the written notice required under (f-1) if the court finds that failure to do so would cause an inequitable or unjust result for the parties. Additionally, any subsection (b) contracts that were executed prior to the effective date are presumed properly exe- cuted if an action to void or invalidate the contract was not filed prior to the effective date of the bill. The process typically goes like this: The business entity must use the TEC online application to enter the required information onto Form 1295, print a copy, and file that copy with the city by the time they submit the signed contract to the city. The city must then use the TEC online application to acknowledge that they have received Form 1295 not later than 30 days after they receive it. If you are a business entity filling out the form, use form CERT-BUS, and if you are an agent of the governmental entity or state agency that received the state contract and wish to acknowledge it, use form CERT-GOV. The Texas Ethics Commission notes that the Form 1295 in the TEC online system does not capture the date of birth or street address of the signatory and as such they will not appear on forms that are filed via the TEC electronic filing system. However, the law does require an unsworn declaration which includes these items. The contracting state agency/governmental agency will keep a physical copy of the form that includes the date of birth and address infor- mation. Whether or not that information is public information is a question for the Office of the Attorney General. While the definition of ΓÇ£governmental entityΓÇ¥ is defined above, it is unclear whether or not public nonprofit corpo- rations like economic development corporations would be considered governmental entities under this section and would be required to comply. Likewise, the term ΓÇ£business entityΓÇ¥ does not (according to TEC Rule ┬º46.3) include other governmental entities, so interlocal agreements between cities would not trigger this disclosure requirement. Section 140.0045, Local Government Code Sec. 140.0045. ITEMIZATION OF CERTAIN PUBLIC NOTICE EXPENDITURES REQUIRED IN CERTAIN POLITICAL SUBDIVISION BUDGETS. (a) 	Except as provided by Subsection (b), the proposed budget of a political subdivision must include, in a manner allowing for as clear a comparison as practicable between those expenditures in the proposed budget and actual expenditures for the same purpose in the preceding year, a line item indicating expenditures for: (1) 	notices required by law to be published in a newspaper by the political subdivision or a represen- tative of the political subdivision; and (2) 	directly or indirectly influencing or attempting to influence the outcome of legislation or admin- istrative action, as those terms are defined in Section 305.002, Government Code. (b) 	Subsection (a)(1) does not apply to a junior college district. Added by Acts 2017, 85 th Leg., R.S., Ch. 563 (S.B. 622), Sec. 1, eff. June 9, 2017. Amended by Acts 2019, 86 th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1070 (H.B. 1495), Sec. 3, eff. June 14, 2019. P ractice Note This section was added in 2019 amid the much larger fight regarding taxpayer funded lobbying. It requires all political subdivisions except junior college districts to include in their budgets a line item of expenditures for directly or indirectly influencing or attempting to influence the outcome of legislation or administrative action. Additionally, Governmental Entity Reporting T E X A S E T H I C S L A W S 401 while this applies specifically to political subdivisions, if the political subdivision itself is a member of a professional association or if it pays membership fees for any of its individual employees or officers to be part of a professional association, that subdivision will be required to report a pro rata amount of the dues paid to the association which is attributable to lobbying by the association, if any. Section 161.107, Local Government Code Sec. 161.107. DISCLOSURE OF CERTAIN CONTRACTS. (a) 	The commission shall prominently display on the countyΓÇÖs Internet website the following regarding contracts for services executed by the county that would require a person to register as a lobbyist under Chapter 305, Government Code: (1) 	the execution dates; (2) 	the contract duration terms, including any extension options; (3) 	the effective dates; (4) 	the final amount of money the county paid in the previous fiscal year; (5) 	the identity of all parties to the contract; (6) 	the identity of all subcontractors in the contract; and (7) 	the legislative agenda of the county. (b) 	In lieu of displaying the items described by Subsections (a)(1)-(6) regarding a contract for services that would require a person to register as a lobbyist under Chapter 305, Government Code, the commis- sion may post on the countyΓÇÖs Internet website the contract executed by the county for those services. (c) 	Information required to be displayed on a countyΓÇÖs Internet website under this section is public infor- mation subject to disclosure under Chapter 552, Government Code. Added by Acts 2019, 86 th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1070 (H.B. 1495), Sec. 5, eff. June 14, 2019. P ractice Note This section was also included in the 2019 push to end taxpayer funded lobbying, and now requires substantial information to be posted on county websites about any contract with registered lobbyists and the legislative agenda of the county as well.
